tool.name: npm
tool.tagline: The package manager and registry client that ships with Node.js
tool.description: npm is the package manager bundled with Node.js and the client for the npm registry, the largest package registry in the world. It installs and locks dependency trees, runs project scripts, manages monorepo workspaces and publishes packages, so mastering it means reproducible builds, safer dependencies and smooth releases.

concepts.name: The npm CLI and the registry
concepts.summary: Find your way around the npm CLI: inspect packages with view, see what is installed with ls, and get help for any command.
concepts.why: Knowing a dozen commands well saves hours of guessing about what is installed and why.
concepts.body:
npm is two things: the **registry** at `registry.npmjs.org`, holding millions of packages, and the **CLI** that ships with Node.js. Node 24 bundles npm 11; npm 12 (July 2026) requires Node 22.22+/24.15+ and tightens several defaults, noted where relevant in these lessons.

Beyond `install` and `run`, the commands you will use every week:

- `npm view <pkg>`: registry metadata: versions, dist-tags, dependencies, publish dates, repository. `npm view react versions --json` lists every version.
- `npm ls <pkg>`: where a package sits in your installed tree; `npm ls --all` prints the whole tree.
- `npm explain <pkg>` (alias `why`): the chain of dependents that caused it to be installed.
- `npm outdated`: current, wanted and latest versions of your dependencies.
- `npm exec <bin>` / `npx <bin>`: run a package's executable, from `node_modules/.bin` or a temporary download.
- `npm pkg get|set|delete`: read and edit `package.json` fields from scripts without hand-editing JSON.
- `npm doctor`, `npm config list`, `npm help <command>`.

Flags have long and short forms (`--save-dev` / `-D`, `--global` / `-g`). npm 12 is stricter: unknown flags and abbreviated flags are now errors rather than warnings, so spell flags out in scripts.

Global installs (`-g`) put binaries on your PATH but are invisible to the project; prefer `devDependencies` plus `npx` for project tools.
concepts.code:
npm --version                  # 11.x with Node 24
npm view express version       # latest published version, e.g. 5.1.0
npm view express dist-tags     # { latest: '5.1.0', next: '...', ... }
npm view express time.modified # last publish date

npm ls express                 # where it is installed in this project
npm explain debug              # why is "debug" in my tree?
# debug@4.4.0
# node_modules/debug
#   debug@"^4.4.0" from express@5.1.0
#   node_modules/express
#     express@"^5.1.0" from the root project

npm outdated                   # Current / Wanted / Latest per dependency
npm pkg get scripts.test       # read one field of package.json
npx eslint --version           # run a local or temporary binary
takeaways: `npm view` reads registry metadata without installing
`npm ls` and `npm explain` answer what and why
`npx`/`npm exec` run package binaries
npm 12 rejects unknown or abbreviated flags
pitfalls: Installing project tools globally so builds depend on one machine's setup.

quiz.q: Which command shows the chain of packages that pulled a dependency into your tree?
quiz.explain: `npm explain` (alias `npm why`) prints the dependents that require a package.

concepts.name: Version ranges and dist-tags
concepts.summary: Read every semver range form npm accepts, install from dist-tags like next, and decide when to pin exact versions.
concepts.why: Ranges decide which code you actually run after the next install.
concepts.body:
You know `^1.4.2` and `~1.4.2`. npm accepts the full **node-semver** grammar:

- **X-ranges**: `1.x` or `1` (any 1.y.z), `*` (anything).
- **Comparators**: `>=1.2.0 <1.5.0`; combine with spaces (AND) and `||` (OR): `^2.0.0 || ^3.0.0`.
- **Hyphen ranges**: `1.2.3 - 1.4` means `>=1.2.3 <1.5.0`.
- **Prereleases** like `2.0.0-beta.3` sort before `2.0.0` and are only matched by ranges that mention a prerelease of the same `major.minor.patch`. `^1.0.0` never installs `2.0.0-beta.1`.

**Dist-tags** are named pointers to versions. `latest` is what `npm install pkg` gives you; maintainers publish betas under tags like `next` or `beta` so they do not become `latest`. Install one with `npm install react@next`, inspect with `npm view react dist-tags`.

Pinning: `npm install -E pkg` (`--save-exact`) writes `1.4.2` instead of `^1.4.2`; `npm config set save-exact true` makes it the default. Since the lockfile already pins your installed tree, exact ranges mainly matter for tools whose updates you want to adopt deliberately, and for applications that prefer explicit upgrade PRs from bots like Renovate or Dependabot.

Libraries should use ranges (usually `^`) so consumers can deduplicate shared dependencies.
concepts.code:
npx semver -r "^1.4.2" 1.4.1 1.9.0 2.0.0      # 1.9.0
npx semver -r "1.2.3 - 1.4" 1.2.3 1.4.9 1.5.0    # 1.2.3, 1.4.9
npx semver -r "^2.0.0 || ^3.0.0" 2.5.0 3.1.0 4.0.0  # 2.5.0, 3.1.0
npx semver -r "^1.0.0" 2.0.0-beta.1              # (nothing: prerelease excluded)

npm view vite dist-tags          # { latest: '8.x.y', beta: '...', ... }
npm install vite@beta            # install whatever "beta" points to
npm install -E typescript@5.9.3  # writes "typescript": "5.9.3"
npm install 'lodash@>=4.17.21 <5'
takeaways: Ranges: ^, ~, x-ranges, comparators, `||` and hyphen ranges
Prereleases match only ranges that opt into them
Dist-tags (`latest`, `next`, `beta`) are movable pointers
`-E` pins exactly; libraries should keep ranges
pitfalls: Expecting `^1.0.0` to pick up `2.0.0-rc.1`; prereleases of other versions never match.

quiz.explain: A partial upper bound in a hyphen range means `<1.5.0`, so 1.4.9 matches.

concepts.name: package-lock.json and npm ci
concepts.summary: Understand what the lockfile records, when npm install changes it, how npm ci uses it, and how to resolve lockfile merge conflicts.
concepts.why: The lockfile is what makes 'works on my machine' work on every machine.
concepts.body:
`package-lock.json` records the **exact resolved tree**: every package's version, where it was downloaded from (`resolved`) and its content hash (`integrity`). It is generated from `package.json` ranges plus the registry state at install time.

When it changes:

- `npm install` (no arguments) keeps locked versions that still satisfy `package.json`, and only resolves what is new or no longer matches.
- `npm install pkg`, `npm update`, `npm uninstall` change it deliberately.
- `npm ci` never changes it. It deletes `node_modules`, installs exactly the lockfile, and **fails** if `package.json` and the lockfile disagree. Use it in CI, Docker builds and deploys.

Rules of thumb:

- **Commit** the lockfile for applications and libraries alike (it does not affect consumers of a published library; npm ignores lockfiles inside dependencies).
- Never delete it to "fix" an install: you silently upgrade hundreds of transitive packages at once.
- **Merge conflicts**: resolve `package.json` first, then run `npm install`; npm can repair a lockfile with conflict markers. Commit the result.
- Pass `--omit=dev` (or set `NODE_ENV=production`) for production images.

npm 12 removed `npm shrinkwrap`: `npm-shrinkwrap.json` is no longer honoured, so rename it to `package-lock.json` if you still have one.
concepts.code:
# Developer: add a dependency (updates package.json AND the lockfile)
npm install zod
git add package.json package-lock.json

# CI / Docker: exact, clean, reproducible
npm ci                     # fails if package.json and lockfile disagree
npm ci --omit=dev          # production install without devDependencies

# Merge conflict in package-lock.json:
git checkout --theirs package-lock.json   # or fix package.json conflicts first
npm install                               # npm rebuilds a consistent lockfile
git add package-lock.json

# Dockerfile pattern: copy manifests first for layer caching
#   COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
#   RUN npm ci --omit=dev
#   COPY . .
takeaways: The lockfile pins every version, URL and integrity hash
`npm ci` installs exactly the lockfile and never modifies it
Commit it; never delete it to fix problems
Resolve lockfile conflicts by re-running `npm install`
pitfalls: Running `npm install` in CI, which can drift from the reviewed lockfile.

quiz.q: What does `npm ci` do if package.json requires a range the lockfile does not satisfy?
quiz.explain: `npm ci` refuses to proceed when the two files are out of sync.

concepts.name: npm scripts and lifecycle hooks
concepts.summary: Write package.json scripts, pass arguments with --, use pre/post hooks and npm_ environment variables, and run binaries with npm exec.
concepts.why: Scripts are the shared, documented command interface of every JavaScript project.
concepts.body:
The `scripts` field maps names to shell commands. `npm run <name>` executes them with `node_modules/.bin` prepended to `PATH`, so locally installed tools run without global installs. `npm test`, `npm start`, `npm stop` and `npm restart` have shortcuts. `npm run` with no name lists all scripts.

Details worth knowing:

- **Arguments**: everything after `--` is passed to the script: `npm run test -- --watch`.
- **Pre and post hooks**: `prebuild` runs before `build`, `postbuild` after, automatically.
- **Lifecycle scripts** run during other commands: `prepare` (after a local install and before publish), `prepublishOnly`, `preinstall`/`install`/`postinstall` (when a package is installed as a dependency).
- **Environment**: scripts see `npm_package_name`, `npm_package_version`, `npm_lifecycle_event` and more.
- Scripts run in `sh` on Unix and `cmd.exe` on Windows by default, so avoid shell-specific syntax (or set `script-shell`) in cross-platform projects.
- `npm run <script> --workspaces` runs it in every workspace; `--if-present` skips packages without it.

Node 22+ offers `node --run <script>`, which starts faster but skips pre/post hooks and npm's environment variables.

Keep scripts short; move complex logic into a `scripts/*.js` file run with `node`.
takeaways: `npm run` adds node_modules/.bin to PATH
Pass arguments after `--`
pre<name>/post<name> hooks run automatically
`node --run` is faster but skips hooks
pitfalls: Using Bash-only syntax in scripts that Windows contributors must run.

quiz.q: What runs when you type `npm test` and `pretest` is defined?
quiz.explain: npm runs the pre hook first, then the script, then any post hook.

concepts.name: Dependency types: dev, peer, optional
concepts.summary: Choose between dependencies, devDependencies, peerDependencies and optionalDependencies, and install subsets with --omit.
concepts.why: The wrong dependency type bloats production images or breaks your library's users.
concepts.body:
`package.json` has several dependency fields, each with different install behaviour:

- `dependencies`: needed at runtime. Installed for your project and for anyone who installs your package.
- `devDependencies`: needed only to develop, build or test (TypeScript, test runners, linters, bundlers). Installed for your project, never for consumers of a published package. Skip them in production with `npm ci --omit=dev`.
- `peerDependencies`: "I plug into a host package the **consumer** provides." A React component library declares `"react": "^18 || ^19"` as a peer instead of bundling its own React. Since npm 7, missing peers are installed automatically, and conflicting peer ranges fail with `ERESOLVE`. Mark optional peers with `peerDependenciesMeta`.
- `optionalDependencies`: installed if possible; a failure (e.g. a platform-specific native binary) does not fail the install. Your code must handle their absence.
- `bundleDependencies`: shipped inside your package tarball.

For bundled frontend apps the distinction is softer, since the bundler decides what ships; many teams still keep build tools in `devDependencies` for faster CI installs.

`--legacy-peer-deps` ignores peer dependencies entirely and `--force` overrides conflicts. Both hide real incompatibilities; prefer fixing versions or using `overrides`.
takeaways: dependencies ship to consumers; devDependencies never do
peerDependencies: the host provides it (React, plugins)
optionalDependencies may fail to install
Avoid `--legacy-peer-deps` and `--force` as permanent fixes
pitfalls: Listing react as a regular dependency in a component library, causing two React copies.

quiz.q: A Vite plugin needs the consumer's own copy of `vite`. Where should `vite` go?
quiz.explain: Plugins plug into the host's instance, so vite is a peer; it is also a devDependency to test locally.

concepts.name: Updating dependencies safely
concepts.summary: Keep dependencies current with outdated, update and targeted major upgrades, deduplicate the tree, and automate with bots.
concepts.why: Stale dependencies accumulate vulnerabilities and painful multi-major upgrades.
concepts.body:
A healthy routine:

- `npm outdated` shows **Current** (installed), **Wanted** (newest within your range) and **Latest** (the `latest` dist-tag). Red rows are behind what your range allows.
- `npm update` moves everything to **Wanted** and updates the lockfile. Safe-ish: same majors (for `^` ranges).
- Major upgrades are explicit: `npm install pkg@latest`, then read the changelog and run the tests. Upgrade one major at a time for big frameworks.
- `npm dedupe` simplifies the tree by moving shared dependencies up so fewer duplicate versions are installed; `npm find-dupes` previews it.
- `npm install --before=2026-09-01` or the `min-release-age` setting (number of days) resolves only versions published before a date, which helps reproduce old installs and lets you avoid brand-new, possibly compromised releases.

Automate it: **Renovate** or **Dependabot** open pull requests for updates, group related packages, and can automerge patch updates that pass CI. Keep the lockfile in those PRs so CI tests exactly what will ship.

Transitive dependencies update through their parents' ranges. If a vulnerable transitive package is pinned by a parent you cannot upgrade, use `overrides` (advanced lesson).
concepts.code:
npm outdated
# Package     Current  Wanted  Latest  Location
# express       5.0.1   5.1.0   5.1.0  node_modules/express
# typescript    5.8.3   5.9.3   5.9.3  node_modules/typescript
# vitest        3.2.4   3.2.4   4.0.8  node_modules/vitest

npm update                     # express -> 5.1.0, typescript -> 5.9.3
npm install vitest@latest      # deliberate major upgrade, then run tests
npm test

npm find-dupes                 # what npm dedupe would change
npm dedupe

# Only accept versions that have been public for at least 3 days
npm config set min-release-age 3 --location=project
takeaways: outdated: Current vs Wanted (in range) vs Latest
`npm update` stays within ranges; majors need `pkg@latest`
`npm dedupe` removes duplicate versions
Bots (Renovate, Dependabot) keep updates small and continuous
pitfalls: Letting dependencies rot for two years, then facing five breaking majors at once.

quiz.q: `npm outdated` shows Wanted 5.9.3 and Latest 6.0.0 with range `^5.8.0`. What does `npm update` install?
quiz.explain: `npm update` moves to the newest version that satisfies the declared range.

concepts.name: .npmrc, scopes and private registries
concepts.summary: Configure npm per project, user and machine with .npmrc, route scopes to private registries, and pass auth tokens safely.
concepts.why: Companies install from private registries, and CI needs credentials without leaking them.
concepts.body:
npm reads configuration from several places, highest priority first: command-line flags, environment variables (`npm_config_<key>`), the **project** `.npmrc` (next to `package.json`), the **user** `~/.npmrc`, the global `$PREFIX/etc/npmrc`, and built-in defaults. `npm config list` shows the merged result and where each value came from.

**Scopes** are namespaces like `@acme/ui`. Route a scope to a different registry:

```ini
@acme:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com
```

Everything else still comes from the default `registry`.

**Authentication** is configured per registry host with `//host/:_authToken=...`. Never commit real tokens. Reference an environment variable instead, which npm expands at runtime: `//npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}`. Then CI provides `NPM_TOKEN` as a secret. Logging in interactively (`npm login --registry=...`) writes tokens to the user `.npmrc`, not the project one.

Other useful project settings: `engine-strict=true` (fail on unsupported Node versions in `engines`), `save-exact=true`, `min-release-age`, and `audit-level`.

Registry mirrors and proxies (Verdaccio, Artifactory, Nexus, GitHub Packages, AWS CodeArtifact) cache public packages and host private ones. npm 12 errors on unknown `.npmrc` keys, so typos no longer pass silently.
concepts.code:
# .npmrc in the project root (committed: no secrets, only references)
@acme:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com
//npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=${NODE_AUTH_TOKEN}
engine-strict=true
save-exact=true
min-release-age=3

# Inspect the effective configuration and its sources
npm config list
npm config get registry                 # https://registry.npmjs.org/
npm config get @acme:registry           # https://npm.pkg.github.com

# CI: provide the token as an environment secret
NODE_AUTH_TOKEN=$GITHUB_TOKEN npm ci
takeaways: Config layers: CLI > env > project > user > global > defaults
Route scopes with `@scope:registry=`
Use `${ENV_VAR}` in .npmrc instead of literal tokens
npm 12 rejects unknown config keys
pitfalls: Committing a .npmrc that contains a literal `_authToken` value.

quiz.q: How should a committed project .npmrc provide a registry token?
quiz.explain: npm expands environment variables in .npmrc, so the secret stays in CI settings.

concepts.name: Publishing a package
concepts.summary: Prepare a package with files and metadata, preview it with npm pack, bump versions with npm version, and publish with dist-tags.
concepts.why: Shipping a library or internal package requires a clean, intentional tarball.
concepts.body:
Before publishing, decide **what goes in the tarball**. Use the `files` allow-list in `package.json` (e.g. `["dist"]`) rather than relying on `.npmignore`; `package.json`, `README` and `LICENSE` are always included. Preview with `npm pack --dry-run`, which lists every file and the size. Leaked `.env` files and test fixtures are common mistakes.

Required metadata: a unique `name` (scoped names like `@you/pkg` avoid collisions), `version`, and ideally `description`, `license`, `repository`, `engines`, plus entry points (`exports`, covered later).

Versioning: `npm version patch|minor|major` bumps `version`, commits and tags in Git (`v1.2.4`), running `preversion`/`version`/`postversion` scripts. Use `npm version prerelease --preid=beta` for betas.

Publishing:

- `npm publish` uploads to the registry and moves the `latest` dist-tag. Scoped packages default to restricted (private) access; pass `--access public` the first time you publish an open-source one.
- Publish prereleases with `--tag next` so they do not become `latest`.
- `prepublishOnly` is the place to run build and tests.
- Accounts need 2FA; automation should use **trusted publishing** from CI rather than long-lived tokens (later lesson).

Mistakes: `npm deprecate pkg@1.2.3 "reason"` warns users; `npm unpublish` is only freely allowed within 72 hours (and when nothing depends on the version) and is discouraged, and a version number can never be reused.
concepts.code:
# package.json (excerpt):
#   "name": "@ann/slugify", "version": "1.0.0",
#   "files": ["dist"], "license": "MIT",
#   "scripts": { "build": "tsc", "prepublishOnly": "npm run build && npm test" }

npm pack --dry-run
# npm notice package: @ann/slugify@1.0.0
# npm notice 1.1kB LICENSE
# npm notice 642B  README.md
# npm notice 2.3kB dist/index.js
# npm notice 812B  package.json
# npm notice total files: 4

npm version minor               # 1.0.0 -> 1.1.0, git commit + tag v1.1.0
npm publish --access public     # first publish of a public scoped package
git push --follow-tags

npm version prerelease --preid=beta   # 1.1.1-beta.0
npm publish --tag next                # latest stays at 1.1.0
takeaways: Use `files` and check `npm pack --dry-run` before publishing
`npm version` bumps, commits and tags
Publish prereleases under a non-latest dist-tag
Versions can never be reused; deprecate instead of unpublishing
pitfalls: Publishing a beta without `--tag`, making it the version everyone installs.

options: Without it, the beta becomes the `latest` dist-tag
quiz.explain: npm moves `latest` on every publish unless you choose another tag.

concepts.name: Workspaces and monorepos
concepts.summary: Manage several packages in one repository with npm workspaces: one install, one lockfile, linked local packages and per-workspace commands.
concepts.why: Monorepos are the norm for apps with shared libraries, and workspaces are npm's built-in support.
concepts.body:
**Workspaces** let one root `package.json` manage several packages in subfolders:

```json
{ "name": "acme", "private": true, "workspaces": ["packages/*", "apps/*"] }
```

Running `npm install` at the root installs all workspaces' dependencies into one root `node_modules`, writes **one lockfile**, and **symlinks** each workspace there, so `apps/web` can `import "@acme/ui"` and get the local source without publishing.

Working with them:

- Target one workspace with `-w`: `npm install zod -w apps/api`, `npm run build -w @acme/ui`.
- Run in all: `npm run test --workspaces --if-present` (`-ws` for short).
- Add a dependency between workspaces by name and version: `npm install @acme/ui -w apps/web`; npm links the local copy when the version matches.
- `npm ls -w apps/web` shows one workspace's tree.

Limitations: npm runs workspace scripts in order but has no task graph, caching or "only what changed" logic. Larger monorepos layer **Turborepo** or **Nx** on top, or use **pnpm** workspaces, whose strict, linked `node_modules` prevents packages from importing dependencies they did not declare.

Mark the root `"private": true` so it can never be published by accident.
concepts.code:
# Layout:  package.json (root)  packages/ui/package.json  apps/web/package.json
cat package.json
# { "name": "acme", "private": true,
#   "workspaces": ["packages/*", "apps/*"],
#   "scripts": { "test": "npm run test --workspaces --if-present" } }

npm install                          # one install, one package-lock.json
ls -l node_modules/@acme/            # ui -> ../../packages/ui (symlink)

npm install @acme/ui -w apps/web     # local package as a dependency
npm install -D vitest -w packages/ui # dev dependency of one workspace
npm run build -w @acme/ui            # run one workspace's script
npm run test -ws --if-present        # run everywhere it exists
npm ls -w apps/web --depth=0
takeaways: Root `workspaces` globs list member packages
One install, one lockfile, symlinked local packages
`-w <name>` targets one workspace, `-ws` all of them
Add Turborepo/Nx for task graphs and caching
pitfalls: Forgetting `"private": true` on the root and publishing the whole monorepo by accident.

quiz.q: How does `apps/web` get the local `@acme/ui` code without publishing it?
options: npm copies the source on every build
npm symlinks the workspace into node_modules
quiz.explain: Workspaces are linked into the root node_modules as symlinks.

concepts.name: Auditing and overriding dependencies
concepts.summary: Read npm audit reports, fix vulnerabilities with audit fix or targeted upgrades, and force transitive versions with overrides.
concepts.why: Most vulnerabilities live in transitive dependencies you never chose directly.
concepts.body:
`npm audit` sends your dependency tree to the registry's advisory database and lists known vulnerabilities with severity, the vulnerable range and the dependency path. `npm install` prints a summary automatically.

Fixing, in order of preference:

- `npm audit fix`: upgrades within your declared ranges. Safe to run.
- Upgrade the direct dependency that pulls in the vulnerable package (use `npm explain <pkg>` to find it).
- `npm audit fix --force` may install **breaking** major versions. Review its plan, never run it blindly in CI.
- **overrides**: in the root `package.json`, force a version anywhere in the tree, or only under one parent:

```json
"overrides": { "semver": "^7.5.4", "jest": { "micromatch": "^4.0.8" } }
```

Overrides only work in the root project (not in published packages). Use `$name` to reference your own direct dependency's version and keep them in sync. Remove overrides once upstream fixes land.

Triage matters: an advisory in a dev-only build tool that never sees untrusted input is lower risk than one in your HTTP parser. Use `npm audit --omit=dev` to focus on what ships, and `--audit-level=high` in CI to fail only above a threshold.

`npm audit signatures` verifies registry signatures and provenance attestations of installed packages.
concepts.code:
npm audit
# semver  <7.5.2
# Severity: moderate
# semver vulnerable to Regular Expression Denial of Service
# fix available via `npm audit fix`
# node_modules/old-lib/node_modules/semver
#   old-lib  *  Depends on vulnerable versions of semver

npm audit fix                       # in-range upgrades only
npm explain semver                  # who depends on it?
npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high   # CI gate on shipped code

# package.json: force a patched version for all or one subtree
#   "overrides": {
#     "semver": "^7.6.0",
#     "old-lib": { "semver": "^7.6.0" }
#   }
npm install && npm ls semver        # verify every copy is patched
npm audit signatures                # verify registry signatures/provenance
takeaways: `npm audit fix` stays in range; `--force` can break things
Upgrade the direct parent first, overrides as a last resort
Overrides only work in the root package.json
Gate CI on shipped code with `--omit=dev --audit-level`
pitfalls: Running `npm audit fix --force` in CI and shipping surprise major upgrades.

quiz.q: A vulnerable transitive package is pinned by an unmaintained parent. Which tool forces a patched version?
quiz.explain: Overrides replace a package's version anywhere in the tree from the root project.

concepts.name: Package entry points: exports and types
concepts.summary: Define a package's public API with the exports field, conditional exports for ESM, CommonJS and types, and subpath imports.
concepts.why: The exports map controls what consumers can import, and mistakes break bundlers, Node and TypeScript differently.
concepts.body:
The `exports` field in `package.json` defines a package's **public entry points**. Once present, consumers can import **only** the listed paths; deep imports like `pkg/dist/internal.js` fail with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`. That encapsulation lets you refactor internals freely.

```json
"exports": {
  ".": { "types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "import": "./dist/index.js", "require": "./dist/index.cjs" },
  "./utils": "./dist/utils.js",
  "./package.json": "./package.json"
}
```

**Conditions** are matched in object order, first match wins: `types` (TypeScript), `import`, `require`, `node`, `browser`, `development`/`production`, and `default` as the fallback. Put `types` first and `default` last.

Related fields:

- `main` and `module` are the legacy entry points; keep `main` only for old tools.
- `type: "module"` makes `.js` files ESM; `.cjs` and `.mjs` override per file.
- `imports` defines private aliases starting with `#`, like `"#db": "./src/db/index.js"`, usable only inside the package.
- `sideEffects: false` tells bundlers unused modules can be dropped entirely.

Dual ESM/CommonJS packages risk the **dual package hazard**: two copies of module state loaded at once. Since Node 22 can `require()` ESM, publishing ESM-only is increasingly viable. Check your package with `publint` and `@arethetypeswrong/cli`.
takeaways: `exports` defines the only importable paths
Conditions match in order: types first, default last
`imports` gives private `#` aliases inside the package
Validate packages with publint and arethetypeswrong
pitfalls: Putting `types` after `import` in a condition object, so TypeScript never sees it.

quiz.q: A package has an `exports` map without `./dist/*`. What happens on `import 'pkg/dist/a.js'`?
quiz.explain: With `exports`, only the declared subpaths are accessible.

concepts.name: Trusted publishing and provenance
concepts.summary: Publish from CI with OIDC trusted publishing instead of long-lived tokens, and attach provenance so users can verify where a package was built.
concepts.why: Stolen publish tokens are behind many npm supply-chain attacks.
concepts.body:
Classic automation published with long-lived tokens stored as CI secrets. Leak one and an attacker can publish malware under your name. The registry now offers better options:

**Trusted publishing** (OIDC): you register a trust relationship between the package and a CI workflow (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD and others) on npmjs.com or with `npm trust github ...` (npm 11.15+). In CI, `npm publish` exchanges the CI provider's short-lived OIDC identity token for a publish credential. There is no npm token to store, rotate or leak. In GitHub Actions the job needs `permissions: id-token: write`.

**Provenance**: packages published from supported CI with trusted publishing get a signed **provenance attestation** automatically (or use `npm publish --provenance` with token-based CI publishing). It links the tarball to the source repository, commit and workflow that built it, recorded in the public Sigstore transparency log. The npm website shows a provenance badge; consumers verify with `npm audit signatures`.

**Staged publishing** (`npm stage publish`) lets CI upload a version that stays unavailable until a maintainer approves it with 2FA, restoring a human check for automated releases.

Also: require 2FA for publishing in package settings, prefer granular access tokens with short expiry where tokens are unavoidable, and limit maintainers.
concepts.code:
# .github/workflows/release.yml
name: release
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write          # lets npm obtain a GitHub OIDC token
jobs:
  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
          registry-url: https://registry.npmjs.org
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm publish --access public   # no NPM_TOKEN: trusted publishing + provenance
takeaways: Trusted publishing swaps CI OIDC tokens for publish rights: no stored secret
Provenance links a tarball to its repo, commit and workflow
Staged publishing adds a 2FA approval to automated releases
Consumers verify with `npm audit signatures`
pitfalls: Keeping a long-lived automation token in CI secrets after moving to trusted publishing.

quiz.q: What does a provenance attestation let consumers verify?
options: That the code has no bugs
Which repository, commit and CI workflow built the package
quiz.explain: Provenance is a signed statement about the build's source and pipeline.

concepts.name: How npm builds node_modules
concepts.summary: Understand npm's ideal tree, hoisting and duplication, phantom dependencies, install strategies, and how pnpm differs.
concepts.why: Most mysterious install bugs come from how the tree is laid out on disk.
concepts.body:
npm's installer (**Arborist**) works in phases: load the **actual tree** (what is in `node_modules`) and the lockfile, compute an **ideal tree** that satisfies every range, then **reify**: diff the two and add, remove or move packages on disk.

Node resolves `require("x")` by walking up `node_modules` folders, and npm exploits that with **hoisting** (the default `install-strategy=hoisted`): each package is placed as high as possible, ideally at the root, so it can be shared. When two packages need incompatible versions, one copy is hoisted and the other is nested under its dependent: `node_modules/a/node_modules/lodash`.

Consequences:

- **Phantom dependencies**: your code can import a hoisted package you never declared. It works until a parent stops depending on it. Lint for undeclared imports.
- **Duplicates**: several versions of the same package can coexist; `npm ls pkg` and `npm dedupe` reveal and reduce them. Duplicated singletons (React, a GraphQL library) cause "multiple instances" errors.
- The layout depends on install order and history, which the lockfile pins.

Alternative strategies: `nested` (no hoisting), `shallow` (only direct deps at the top), and `linked`, which stores packages in `node_modules/.store` and symlinks them, similar to **pnpm**. pnpm's content-addressable store and strict, symlinked layout save disk space and eliminate phantom dependencies; Yarn PnP drops `node_modules` entirely.
concepts.code:
mkdir layout-demo && cd layout-demo && npm init -y >/dev/null
npm install express@5 --silent
npm ls debug --all
# layout-demo@1.0.0
# └─┬ express@5.3.0
#   ├─┬ body-parser@2.3.0
#   │ └── debug@4.4.3 deduped
#   ├── debug@4.4.3
#   ...
ls node_modules | wc -l        # ~65 packages hoisted to the top level
node -e "require('debug')"     # works: a phantom dependency!

npm install --install-strategy=linked --silent
ls -A node_modules             # only express (+ .store, .package-lock.json)
node -e "require('debug')"     # Error: Cannot find module 'debug'
takeaways: Arborist: actual tree + lockfile -> ideal tree -> reify
Hoisting shares packages but enables phantom dependencies
Conflicting versions are nested under their dependents
`linked` strategy and pnpm give strict, symlinked layouts
pitfalls: Importing a package that only exists because another dependency pulled it in.

quiz.q: Why can code `require()` a package not listed in its package.json under the default npm layout?
options: npm adds it to package.json automatically
It was hoisted to the root node_modules by another dependency
quiz.explain: Hoisting makes transitive dependencies visible at the top level.

concepts.name: Inside package-lock.json
concepts.summary: Read lockfileVersion 3: the packages map keyed by install path, resolved URLs, integrity hashes, flags, and the hidden lockfile.
concepts.why: Reading the lockfile directly answers questions no command does, and lets you review dependency changes in PRs.
concepts.body:
Modern npm writes **lockfileVersion 3**. Its core is a `packages` object keyed by **install location**:

- `""` is the root project, repeating its dependency ranges.
- `"node_modules/express"` is a hoisted package; `"node_modules/a/node_modules/lodash"` a nested one. Workspaces appear by folder (`"packages/ui"`) plus a `link: true` entry under `node_modules`.

Each entry records:

- `version` and `resolved`: the exact tarball URL. For private registries this reveals where packages come from.
- `integrity`: a Subresource Integrity hash, normally `sha512-...`. npm verifies every downloaded tarball against it, so a tampered registry or mirror is detected.
- `dependencies`, `peerDependencies`, `optionalDependencies` ranges as declared by that package, and `engines`, `os`, `cpu`, `bin`, `license`.
- Flags: `dev: true`, `optional: true`, `devOptional: true`, `peer: true`, `hasInstallScript: true` (a quick way to list packages that run install scripts).

npm also keeps a **hidden lockfile** at `node_modules/.package-lock.json`, a cache of the actual tree that speeds up later installs.

The example is abridged. Reviewing lockfile diffs in PRs is real security work: unexpected `resolved` hosts, git URLs or new `hasInstallScript` packages deserve a closer look. Tools like `lockfile-lint` automate host and scheme checks.
takeaways: `packages` is keyed by install path, root is ""
`integrity` hashes are verified on every download
Flags like dev, optional and hasInstallScript classify entries
Review lockfile diffs: hosts, git URLs, install scripts
pitfalls: Approving PRs without looking at lockfile changes, where malicious URLs hide.

quiz.q: What does npm do with the `integrity` field?
options: Uses it as a cache key only
Verifies the downloaded tarball's hash against it
quiz.explain: A mismatch means the tarball differs from what was locked, and the install fails.

concepts.name: Defending against supply-chain attacks
concepts.summary: Control install scripts with allowScripts, restrict git and URL dependencies, delay fresh releases, and harden CI installs.
concepts.why: Malicious package versions and install scripts are the most common way attackers reach developer machines and CI.
concepts.body:
Real attacks on the npm ecosystem follow a few patterns: **typosquatting** (`expresss`), **compromised maintainer accounts** publishing malicious versions of popular packages, **dependency confusion** (a public package with the name of your private one), and **install scripts** that steal tokens the moment you run `npm install`.

Defences built into npm:

- **Install script policy.** The `allowScripts` field in `package.json` lists which dependencies may run `preinstall`/`install`/`postinstall`. Manage it with `npm approve-scripts` and `npm deny-scripts`. In npm 11 it is advisory (installs report unreviewed scripts); **npm 12 blocks unreviewed dependency install scripts by default**. `--ignore-scripts` disables them entirely.
- **Git and URL dependencies**: `allow-git` and `allow-remote` limit them; npm 12 defaults both to `none`.
- **Cooling-off period**: `min-release-age=3` (days) avoids versions published minutes ago, the window in which most malicious releases are caught and removed.
- **Scoped private packages** routed to your registry prevent dependency confusion.
- `npm ci` with a reviewed lockfile, `npm audit signatures`, and provenance checks.

Around npm: run CI installs with no secrets in the environment, give publish jobs separate minimal permissions, use trusted publishing, and consider package firewalls or scanners (Socket, Snyk, GitHub dependency review) that flag suspicious new versions.
takeaways: Attacks: typosquats, hijacked maintainers, dependency confusion, install scripts
`allowScripts` + approve/deny-scripts control install scripts (enforced in npm 12)
Restrict git/URL deps and wait out fresh releases with min-release-age
Keep secrets out of CI install steps
pitfalls: Running `npm install` in CI jobs that also hold deploy credentials in environment variables.

quiz.q: Why does a `min-release-age` of a few days reduce risk?
options: Most malicious releases are detected and removed within that window
quiz.explain: Compromised versions are usually caught quickly, so not installing brand-new releases avoids them.
